_README: DERIVED ARTIFACT - do not hand-edit. Generated 2026-08-25 from the do-not-print blocks in References/research_*.md and week-plan_*.md accuracy watchlists. The research notes are the source of truth; regenerate rather than editing. See References/DESIGN_brief-radar_2026-08-25.md sec 4.4.

claims.claim: 115,000 tech layoffs through May 2026, approaching all of 2025's 124,000
claims.correction: No source prints exactly 115,000. Use 125,759 (Layoffs.fyi, 6 Aug) or 149,023 (Challenger YTD). 2025 total was 123,941 at 269 companies. Name one tracker; never blend.

claims.claim: "approaching all of 2025's total" (tech layoffs)
claims.correction: Overtaken — 2026 passed the 2025 total in early August.

claims.claim: "Meta, Amazon and Snap citing AI" for their layoffs
claims.correction: Meta and Snap explicit; Amazon framed its cuts as bureaucracy/culture with AI as enabler — say "AI-adjacent," not "citing AI."

claims.claim: the ">165,000" layoffs tracker figure (Yahoo/Engadget)
claims.correction: Inflates by counting multi-year programmes in full (e.g. Oracle's 21,000-over-12-months). Don't use.

claims.claim: Block cut "50% of workforce"
claims.correction: Almost certainly wrong — use ~4,000. (The Block cut is February 2026, six months old.)

claims.claim: "only two executives, each knows half, never fly on the same plane" (Coca-Cola formula)
claims.correction: A myth. Coca-Cola says "a few people"; Snopes/Africa Check rate it false. Usable instead: the recipe spent 86 years in a bank vault before Coca-Cola built it its own shrine.
match_strings: never fly on the same plane

claims.claim: Kimi K3's 93.4% SWE-bench Verified score, printed bare
claims.correction: It is Moonshot's own claim. UK AISI/CAISI published only a preliminary cyber assessment 23 Jul; no independent benchmark verification. Do not print the number bare.

claims.claim: "<3% in the first 12 months" as the comparison baseline for the ~4%/yr AI-exposed contraction
claims.correction: Has no primary — cut it. Use the lab's own "intensified in the nine months since the paper was first released." Verified figures: 3.8%/yr contraction for exposed 22–25s vs +2.0% for least-exposed.

claims.claim: "~6% wage premium at entry level vs 70%+ at senior" attributed to PwC
claims.correction: NOT a PwC figure. The full 2026 Global AI Jobs Barometer PDF was reviewed end to end: no seniority-based wage-premium breakdown anywhere; the only premium is the single aggregate 62%. Keep it out.

claims.claim: the 28–56% AI wage premium set against PwC 2026's 62%
claims.correction: Still unpinned, open since 6 Aug. Pin one figure with a primary or disown the number in text before anything is drafted.

claims.claim: "the federal government failed to deliver on the mandates" / the AI framework deadline lapsed and nothing was delivered
claims.correction: Contradicted by the 3 August 2026 White House statement announcing the voluntary framework. If any of that made it into a draft, cut it.
match_strings: failed to deliver on the mandates

claims.claim: Yahoo Finance / Forkast, "White House AI Framework Deadline Lapses" (Lena Park, 31 July 2026) cited as reporting
claims.correction: Opinion column, no named sources or primary documents. Do not cite. Recycled by KuCoin, Neomanex, Cryptobriefing, Vorp Labs. Note it still ranks first in search.
match_strings: White House AI Framework Deadline Lapses

claims.claim: a ~$10K private-AI box breaks even against cloud inference in 3–6 months at 50,000 queries/month
claims.correction: The 50,000 figure appears in neither source (Petronella says 100K+). Real break-even is ~33 months gross, 50–100 months net of power. 3–6 months needs 280,000–550,000 queries/month. The defensible economic argument is per-seat licensing, not per-token inference.

claims.claim: $4.7M as an AI-related breach cost figure
claims.correction: No primary. Nearest real figure is IBM Cost of a Data Breach 2025: $4.74M for orgs with high shadow-AI levels.

claims.claim: "employees' personal accounts are already in criminal hands"
claims.correction: Not sourced — Okta's finding is largely fraud against providers; Unit 42's is stolen developer keys.

claims.claim: Unit 42's "tens of millions of API calls per day"
claims.correction: An unsourced capability estimate, not a measurement.
match_strings: tens of millions of API calls

claims.claim: "87% use AI"
claims.correction: Glean's own caveat concedes "The sample skews higher on AI adoption, seniority, and digitally intensive sectors," and the population is "digital workers." Bare, it is wrong.

claims.claim: "11 hrs/week saved" as a realised saving
claims.correction: Self-reported counterfactual, scope-limited to "through automation alone" — and contradicted roughly 3:1 by Section's AI Proficiency Report (n=5,000): 68% save four hours or less per week.

claims.claim: "half the savings are reabsorbed"
claims.correction: Arithmetic on two correlated self-reports from the same respondents. Not a measurement. Safe alternative: "6.4 hours a week botsitting" — botsitting is Glean's coinage.

claims.claim: "verification debt, context reconstruction, compliance friction" attributed to the Glean study
claims.correction: These terms do not appear in the Glean report. They are the Substack author's framing. Do not attribute that four-part decomposition to any study.

claims.claim: "1 in 8" (workers helped by AI) without the word "significantly"
claims.correction: Glean measured significantly better. Dropping the adverb converts "not transformative" into "no help at all." The same report says 75% say it makes them more productive.

claims.claim: "Cost-per-Accepted-Task Analyst" as a job title
claims.correction: Zero live postings, zero historical postings, zero named employers across LinkedIn, Indeed, ZipRecruiter, Greenhouse, Lever, Ashby. It is AIDB's descriptive coinage for a function — say so rather than hedging the posting volume. The metric is real and traces to McKinsey's "cost per completed task."

claims.claim: "about 60 percent of an agentic task's costs are tied to refining answers" as McKinsey research
claims.correction: McKinsey's own footnote attributes it to Salim, Latendresse, Khatoonabadi & Shihab, arXiv:2601.14470, 20 Jan 2026 — and the paper says 59.4%, measured on agentic software-engineering workflows only.

claims.claim: "agentic work costs 5–30x a simple chat" attributed to McKinsey
claims.correction: McKinsey says something different in both directions (~1,000x tokens vs chat; factor-of-30 variance between runs of the same task). The 5–30x traces to Gartner, March 2026, reached only through vendor blogs. Treat as unverified.

claims.claim: "The company consensus is that orgs that rushed to lay people off for AI savings are finding they need to re-hire for senior roles."
claims.correction: "Company consensus" is not an attribution. Must not enter a draft in this form — replace with Robert Half or Orgvue, named and dated.

claims.claim: August 2026 Patch Tuesday as "421 CVEs, 62 critical, 357 important"
claims.correction: The three figures come from incompatible counts and do not sum (421 − 62 = 359). 421 = Rapid7/SecurityWeek · 418 = SANS ISC · 400 = BleepingComputer · 398 = ZDI/Tenable. There is no primary count; MSRC publishes no total. Write "roughly 400" or "398–421 depending on who is counting," and name the counter.

claims.claim: August 2026 Patch Tuesday was a "record"
claims.correction: July 2026 was the record at 570. Aug 2025 was 107 — roughly 3.7–3.9x year-on-year, which is the defensible framing and sharper than "record."
claims.match_note: "record" alone is generic — pair it with 570/107 or with a Patch Tuesday context match.

claims.claim: "Patch Tuesday volumes tripled in 2026"
claims.correction: Jan 113 vs Aug 398 is month variance, not a trend.

claims.claim: CVE-2026-62878 (Windows DNS Server) described as "wormable"
claims.correction: "Wormable" appears nowhere in Microsoft's advisory — it is ZDI's word and must be attributed in the same sentence. Microsoft's record: Exploited No · Publicly Disclosed No · "Exploitation Less Likely," attacker "could" exploit. Microsoft rates WDS TFTP (CVE-2026-62893) more likely than DNS.

claims.claim: enumerating the August 2026 CVSS 9.8 unauthenticated RCEs as a closed list of three
claims.correction: There are four, not three — DNS (CVE-2026-62878), QUIC (CVE-2026-62815), WDS TFTP (CVE-2026-62893); the fourth is unpinned. Do not enumerate as a closed list.

claims.claim: CVE-2026-68820 characterised as a remote / unauthenticated / wormable RCE, Critical severity
claims.correction: It is an elevation of privilege: "Use after free in Windows Ancillary Function Driver for WinSock allows an authorized attacker to elevate privileges locally." CVSS 7.0 (AV:L/AC:H/PR:L), Important not Critical, "requires an attacker to win a race condition." Exploited: Yes; KEV cisaExploitAdd 2026-08-11, due 2026-08-25 under BOD 26-04. "Zero-day" is accurate.

claims.claim: any sentence containing "Task Host," "April," "ransomware" or "confirmed" against CVE-2026-68820
claims.correction: Four assertions refuted; the KEV ransomware field is Unknown. This was the second consecutive regeneration of the same CVE with a bigger claim each time.

claims.claim: attributing CVE-2026-68820 exploitation to Lazarus / Operation Dream Job as CISA's or Microsoft's finding
claims.correction: The Lazarus / Dream Job attribution is Check Point Research's, not CISA's and not Microsoft's.

claims.claim: vCenter "mass-compromised within five days"
claims.correction: CVE-2026-59310. 361 victim IPs (not hosts, not organisations) from QUIRSO GmbH, methodology undisclosed; their own caveat says an IP "does not necessarily correspond to a unique company or physical system." Five days = time to first observed exploitation (29 Jul advisory → 3 Aug). APT is "suspected" and unnamed. Not in CISA KEV; Broadcom acknowledges no exploitation.

claims.claim: Adobe Commerce CVE-2026-71362 "under active exploit"
claims.correction: Adobe's own bulletin APSB26-92 (11 Aug, priority 2): "Adobe is not aware of any exploits in the wild for any of the issues addressed in these updates." The exploitation claim is Sansec's, which sells the Magento WAF. Blocked WAF attempts are not compromise. Not in KEV.
CVSS is 9.1. BleepingComputer prints 9.8 — do not inherit it.

claims.claim: Gunra ransomware hit "nine sectors" and expanded its sector spread
claims.correction: Ten sectors are named in joint advisory AA26-222A (10 Aug 2026, FBI/CISA/DC3/NSA/USSS/Korean NPA), and the expansion sentence is about the RaaS affiliate programme, not sector spread. No total victim count is given.

claims.claim: "Gunra: 80+ victims, since mid-2026"
claims.correction: Neither figure is in AA26-222A. Gunra was first observed April 2025.

claims.claim: Darktrace's percentages presented as incidence — "top AI-driven threats are…"
claims.correction: They are self-reported worries: "50% of security leaders mentioned hyper-personalized phishing campaigns as one of their biggest worries"; 45% listed automated vulnerability scanning among biggest concerns; 40% adaptive malware; 40% deepfake voice fraud.

claims.claim: "67% have deployed agentic AI for security ops"
claims.correction: Verbatim: "67% report that theirs uses agentic AI" — i.e. present in tooling, vendor-supplied features included. Denominator ambiguous (if the base is the 77% with AI in the stack, the absolute is ~52%). Population "over 1,500 security leaders"; regions, recruitment, fieldwork provider and dates not disclosed.

claims.claim: "State of AI Cybersecurity 2026" attributed to the Cloud Security Alliance
claims.correction: It is Darktrace's report; the CSA blog says "Originally published by Darktrace." A vendor survey laundered into an industry-body finding — by a vendor selling both the detection tooling and the agentic SOC product whose adoption it measures.

claims.claim: the Aura breach attributed to ShinyHunters
claims.correction: A name collision. Wikipedia's actor citations all belong to ShinyHunters' Salesforce Aura campaign against the /s/sfsites/aura endpoint. Aura named no actor and no intrusion date. Drop the Wikipedia citation entirely; it is carrying the error. (Attribution IS sound for Questel — do not let that bleed backwards.)

claims.claim: the Aura breach as ~900,000 customer records
claims.correction: "Approximately 900,000 records" is a marketing contact list "almost exclusively from a company that Aura acquired five years ago"; identifiable customers are <20,000 active + <15,000 former. One employee, ~one hour of access. "No Social Security numbers, passwords, or financial information."

claims.claim: "Allie K. Miller runs 34 proactive agents"
claims.correction: LIFTED 2026-08-23 — the corpus was wrong. The number is real and hers, and it is also the headline figure on the landing page selling her $297 AI-First Academy and paid Agent Mastermind. Attribute, and name the $297 course in the same breath. (Killed 14 Aug as "no primary states 34"; the verification pass had missed her own domain, her own captions and a podcast episode published two days earlier — the corpus's first KILLED-CLAIM FALSE POSITIVE.)

claims.claim: a Greg Isenberg episode with Allie K. Miller with ~29K views
claims.correction: LIFTED 2026-08-23. Killed 14 Aug as "the cited artifact does not exist" — the agent-workforce video that does exist is The Information's, 28 Jun 2026, with 1,524 views.

claims.claim: the AI chief of staff "Simon," the assistant "Toby," six Friends-named directors, and "escalate only what needs her"
claims.correction: LIFTED 2026-08-23 along with the 34-agent figure. Attribute, and name the $297 course in the same breath.

claims.claim: Allie Miller's Stripe / calendar / email / transcripts access list
claims.correction: STILL DO-NOT-PRINT after the 23 Aug lift. Stripe appears in no primary and she argues the opposite: "You're not going to give it email access… start with read-only access and then earn trust." The list traces to one untraceable caption.
match_strings: read-only access and then earn trust

claims.claim: "do smart things" as an Allie Miller quotation
claims.correction: STILL DO-NOT-PRINT after the 23 Aug lift. It appears only in AI-generated aggregator summaries. If used: "a three-word prompt she has described but which I have not found her stating in her own words."

claims.claim: "Codex Browser Use automates literally anything"
claims.correction: OpenAI's own tense refutes it — they will "expand it so Codex can fully command the browser beyond web applications." No OpenAI changelog entry for "Browser Use" exists. Defensible framing: "the automation floor dropped for supervised, non-credentialed GUI work."

claims.claim: "'What should I learn' is converging on orchestration" / the meta-skills consensus
claims.correction: No evidence base. Four searches targeting r/ExperiencedDevs and r/cscareerquestions surfaced zero actual threads; every returned source sells orchestration training. Cut, don't hedge. The only honest form is first-person and unquantified.

claims.claim: "Orchestrator is widening to every function"
claims.correction: Second regeneration of the 14 Aug kill. No evidence base.

claims.claim: "Highest-value gap" / "the defensive hire every enterprise needs"
claims.correction: Unsourced superlatives.

claims.claim: "The architecture-of-work model is a hiring taxonomy"
claims.correction: No named employer, anywhere.

claims.claim: "New adversarial evaluation frameworks" shipped
claims.correction: Nothing shipped and no referent exists. OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications 2026 is a risk taxonomy, not a runnable benchmark; AgentDojo, BIPIA, CyberSecEval predate the window. The real event is the UK AISI incident report, already spent Mon 10 Aug.

claims.claim: Cursor cloud agents are "3x faster"
claims.correction: Cursor's own words: "it starts in a ready environment so you get a response up to 3x faster." Vendor self-measured on their own repos; it measures cold-start elimination via cached environments, not throughput or completion speed. The gain is zero where setup was never the bottleneck.

claims.claim: "Boards are pushing CEOs to move faster on AI" / "60% of boards are pressuring management"
claims.correction: BCG measured CEOs saying boards are rushing them (61%, Split Decisions, May); boards deny it, 54% / 18%. Do not imply this covers listed companies or Australia, and "625 leaders" is not the denominator for the 60%.

claims.claim: "a board-governance newsletter found…" / "industry reporting shows boards…"
claims.correction: The outlet is written by the founder of a company selling board AI tooling (BoardLens), in an edition sponsored by that company. It is never "an industry newsletter reports…" It is the vendor.

claims.claim: "Yale and Brookings independently found…" / "Two independent institutions reached the same conclusion" / "Brookings confirmed Yale's finding"
claims.correction: Same team — Martha Gimbel is Executive Director of the Budget Lab and co-authored the Brookings piece. Safe: "The Brookings analysis was co-written by the Budget Lab's own executive director — same team, same method, second masthead." This is the co-authorship-collapse failure engine.

claims.claim: "Brookings, Hamilton Project and PIIE" presented as three institutions
claims.correction: One Kolko article, one event.

claims.claim: a16z cited as a corroborating source alongside Yale
claims.correction: A synthesis of four papers, one of which is the Yale work cited beside it, with direct portfolio interest in the conclusion. A position, not a confirmation.

claims.claim: "Amodei predicted 10–20% unemployment"
claims.correction: Axios's framing prose, sitting outside the quotation marks, and the verb is "could": "could wipe out half of all entry-level white-collar jobs — and spike unemployment to 10-20%." Three upgrades stacked: could→will, range→ceiling, five-year window→now.

claims.claim: "unusually painful" as an Amodei remark to CNBC about jobs
claims.correction: It is from his own essay and modifies the transition, not jobs.

claims.claim: the "intrinsic property" / wage-insurance / UBI material dated to 5 May 2026
claims.correction: June 2026, a different document.

claims.claim: the Forbes 21 Feb 2026 "doubled down" piece used as a source
claims.correction: Original inaccessible. Cut, or attribute as not-accessed.

claims.claim: "Amodei and Altman both walked back" their displacement warnings ahead of IPO windows
claims.correction: Amodei re-framed (a Jevons argument); only Altman conceded — "my intuitions were just off," Commonwealth Bank conference with Matt Comyn, 26 May 2026. And the filings (1/8 June) postdate the statements (5/26 May): print the sequence, never the causation.

claims.claim: the Amodei 90/10 quote truncated at "if you automate 90% of the job, then everyone does the 10%"
claims.correction: Deleting "expands to be 100%… and 10xs their productivity" inverts a Jevons argument into a concession.

claims.claim: "AI layoffs are a rounding error"
claims.correction: Factually wrong. AI is 23.6% of YTD announced cuts (112,713 of 477,033) and the #1 stated reason five consecutive months — while the total pool is DOWN 41% year on year. Andy Challenger's own honest frame: "AI is still the reason companies give."

claims.claim: BCG's "10–15% eliminated" as a jobs forecast
claims.correction: BCG: "not intended to be an unemployment forecast."
match_strings: not intended to be an unemployment forecast

claims.claim: "BCG's [estimate] is the consensus"
claims.correction: Stanford, OECD and Anthropic's own economist all differ.

claims.claim: "2.5x empathy/judgment/creativity" attributed to BCG
claims.correction: Not in the article. Likely PwC.

claims.claim: "Stanford's estimate rose from 13% to 19%"
claims.correction: Two different estimators charted as one trend line. Like-for-like on the descriptive measure is 15% → 19%. The firm-fixed-effects estimate is no longer headlined: "the firm fixed-effects estimates are more sensitive than the raw descriptive results."

claims.claim: "16%" as the Brynjolfsson early-career gap in the August 2026 revision
claims.correction: 16% appears nowhere in the August 2026 revision. The Lab's own history is 15% (Jul 2025 vintage) → 19% (Jun 2026). Lovett's manuscript cites the earlier vintage — do not blend the two figures or the two windows.

claims.claim: Stanford's "19%" as an absolute decline or an unemployment rate
claims.correction: It is a relative gap between two same-aged groups.

claims.claim: "seniority-biased technological change" attributed to Indeed Hiring Lab
claims.correction: It is Hosseini Maasoum & Lichtinger, SSRN 5425555. Indeed cites it.

claims.claim: ADP payroll data presented as an AI measurement
claims.correction: It contains no AI identification strategy and the source declines the interpretation. And "low-hire, low-fire" is from 14 Oct 2025, not 24 Feb 2026.

claims.claim: "Humlum & Vestergaard rule out effects larger than 1%" under the title "Large Language Models, Small Labor Market Effects"
claims.correction: Withdrawn number, withdrawn title. It is 2%, and the paper is "Still Waters, Rapid Currents."

claims.claim: Acemoglu's TFP figure as 0.71%
claims.correction: The published, peer-reviewed value is 0.66%.

claims.claim: Acemoglu & Restrepo's 0.39pp and 0.2pp presented as competing estimates
claims.correction: Local vs aggregate, from the same paper.

claims.claim: "teller headcount rose until roughly 2007" or the ~500k→~550k figures attributed to Bessen
claims.correction: Not in either Bessen primary. Cite BLS OES directly, or use his tellers-per-branch (20 → 13, 1988–2004) and branch-growth (+43%) numbers.

claims.claim: Brynjolfsson/Li/Raymond's +15% cited as evidence of displacement
claims.correction: It is a productivity result and makes no employment claim. Cite 15%, not 14%.

claims.claim: the OECD sentence quoted without "has been widening since before the pandemic" and without its own "So far"
claims.correction: Both qualifiers must travel with it.

claims.claim: "57% of employers report higher productivity"
claims.correction: They expect it, not report it.

claims.claim: any forecast of the 28 Aug benchmark number
claims.correction: It does not exist yet.

claims.claim: BLS Commissioner status after 20 Jan 2026
claims.correction: Unverified from a BLS primary. Re-check or omit.

claims.claim: "AI displacement is smaller than the error bars"
claims.correction: The defensible form is "an effect of this size could not be detected by these instruments."

claims.claim: any Challenger August 2026 AI-attributed layoff figure
claims.correction: Not published until ~3 Sep 2026 (Challenger August report, 3 Sep 2026, 05:30 ET).

claims.claim: "205,000 AI-linked layoffs in 2026" (Outsource Accelerator / "ResumePulse")
claims.correction: Unestablished tracker, undisclosed inclusion rule, ~82% above Challenger on a similar definition.

claims.claim: "Goldman: AI cost the US 16,000 jobs per month"
claims.correction: It is a reduction in monthly payroll growth, not net losses.

claims.claim: WARN data showing AI causation for layoffs
claims.correction: WARN filings have no reason field.

claims.claim: "that debate is over"
claims.correction: Unsourced, and contradicted by the brief's own Debate section.

claims.claim: "median time to exploit is five days"
claims.correction: Average, not median; 47 days untrimmed; the denominator is already-exploited vulnerabilities.

claims.claim: "time to exploit has gone negative" (unqualified)
claims.correction: One hedged, denominator-free sentence, edge-scoped.

claims.claim: "only 0.24% of vulnerabilities are ever exploited"
claims.correction: Severely time-censored — median publication-to-KEV is 80 days. Gamblin's figure is that 85 of H1 2026's 35,364 CVEs have reached KEV so far.

claims.claim: Windows Resiliency Initiative's "60% faster update adoption"
claims.correction: No denominator, no baseline, no methodology — on a product page selling the licences it justifies.

claims.claim: insurers repricing cyber cover on patch SLA
claims.correction: No primary found.

claims.claim: "OpenAI paused Astra development" / "OpenAI halts Astra"
claims.correction: They paused non-compliant internal activities, not development. Also not "crossed Critical." The safe verb is restructured/paused-specific, never halted.
claims.scope_note: Applies to the pre-Astra-6 August claim only. It does NOT cover the GPT-6.1 Astra release pause reported by ABC News on 30 Sep 2026, which is a separate, live fact (Lars, 1 Oct 2026).

claims.claim: "OpenAI disbanded its preparedness / severe-risk team"
claims.correction: OpenAI denies it on the record — "We have not disbanded the Preparedness team" — and Engadget retracted and apologised. Establishable: Dylan Scandinaro is no longer head of preparedness, and the work is split across bio/cyber/self-improvement leads reporting to head of safety Saachi Jain. The safe verb is restructured, never halted or disbanded.

claims.claim: "Two labs self-reported models outrunning safety controls"
claims.correction: Safeguards were off by design in every case.

claims.claim: "5th senior exit since July"
claims.correction: It is seven, or three. Never five.

claims.claim: "The US told 35 Pax Silica countries to pick a side"
claims.correction: Two instruments (Pax Silica, 24 signatories vs the Joint Statement on AI Opportunity, 35). Reuters is explicit the letter goes to the 35 AI Opportunity signatories — and it is an unsent draft: Reuters "could not establish when Washington will send it." Asserting a completed act is the error. Also: @Countergrind is not a source; cite Reuters or nothing.

claims.claim: Mistral's "€830M" raise
claims.correction: It is US$830M. CNBC, TechCrunch, DCD and Yahoo all say dollars — roughly a €100M+ overstatement.

claims.claim: Mistral "SLA-backed sovereignty"
claims.correction: What exists is an uptime SLA on the paid Priority Tier plus Regional Endpoints ("let customers choose whether their inference runs in Europe or the US") — availability plus a region toggle, not a legal sovereignty guarantee.

claims.claim: Mistral "air-gapped deployment"
claims.correction: No air-gap claim appears in Mistral's announcement or model card.

claims.claim: Mistral Medium 3.5 "runs self-hosted on as few as four GPUs" as a deployment spec
claims.correction: Mistral never says which GPUs or at what quantisation, and its own HF card recommends tensor-parallel-size 8 for serving. An unspecified floor, not a deployment spec. 256K context and modified-MIT open weights are solid.

claims.claim: the Mistral/Eclairion Bruyères-le-Châtel facility described as a running facility
claims.correction: Announced and financed, not operational — and already slipped once (was 18,000 GB200s for summer 2025). 13,800 Nvidia GB300s, 44MW.

claims.claim: "European lab = outside the CLOUD Act"
claims.correction: The test is jurisdiction plus possession/custody/control, not server location. Covington: legal process "can be enforced against any covered technology providers subject to US jurisdiction, regardless of whether the provider is based in the US." Name the commercial interest: the loudest voices on "European = safe" sell European hosting.

claims.claim: "Australia–US CLOUD Act agreement came into force Jan 2026"
claims.correction: January 2024. Year error.

claims.claim: "Google says 340 tok/s" (Gemini 3.7 Flash)
claims.correction: 340.1 tok/s is Artificial Analysis's measurement of the high-thinking variant. Google makes no throughput claim.

claims.claim: Gemini 3.7 Flash is "half the price" (without the expiry date)
claims.correction: $0.75/1M in, $3.75/1M out is introductory, through 31 Dec 2026, reverting to $1.50/$7.50 on 1 Jan 2027. Any "half the price" line needs the expiry date or it is wrong by January.

claims.claim: Gemini 3.7 Flash "benchmarks near Sonnet 5"
claims.correction: Fails both ways. Google's own charts claim 3.7 Flash beats Sonnet 5 on FrontierCode 1.1, DeepSWE v1.1, Code Arena, GDP.pdf and AutomationBench — but these are Google-selected, Google-run, published as chart images, with no SWE-bench Verified number. Safe: "On Google's own charts, using benchmarks Google selected… No independent replication yet."

claims.claim: "Chamath's six layers are… harness…" / the harness definition as his words / "Chamath argues proprietary data + context is where value sits"
claims.correction: The word is not in the 1 May post — layer five is "execution." The August framework is different and its primary is unreachable; the circulating definition is a newsletter's gloss, reaching the intake via a board-directors newsletter quoting a VC newsletter quoting an X post.

claims.claim: "one-person AI business" (Nate Herk) as an achieved state
claims.correction: His own post: "This one person business model is how I started my AI consultancy that we scaled to over $100k/mo. Now obviously in order for me to achieve that scale, I built a team around me." Print the self-refutation.

claims.claim: Coinbase as a clean case of AI displacement
claims.correction: Fortune's own headline says otherwise.

claims.claim: "Cisco says AI will create jobs"
claims.correction: It is one executive's stated belief, not a company position — and he names no study or dataset, hedging then un-hedging two sentences apart. Cisco sells the substrate for AI deployment.
match_strings: create more jobs than it eliminates

claims.claim: a Jack Dorsey quote about "AI agents working with people" (Buzz)
claims.correction: No such statement found. His own words name Slack/GitHub dependency as the motive: "a new groupchat platform for teams of people and agents of all sizes, built to reduce our dependency on slack and github."

claims.claim: any named 2026 AI liability case, or "directors are now liable for AI failures"
claims.correction: There is no decided AI-Caremark case. Oxford Business Law Blog (Mar 2026) cites only pre-existing Delaware authority — Caremark, Stone, Marchand, Clovis, Boeing, McDonald's — and its own verbs are "may." NIS2 Article 20(1) is the one that is actually law.
